questions.question: In OOP, what is a class?
questions.explanation: A class describes the attributes and methods; objects are the individual things built from it.

questions.question: How do you create an object from `class Dog:`?
questions.explanation: Calling the class, `Dog()`, instantiates it. `rex = Dog` would only give the class another name.

questions.question: Two objects created from the same class share their instance attributes.
questions.explanation: Each object has its own instance attributes; only class attributes are shared.

questions.question: What is `self` in a method?
options: The object the method was called on
questions.explanation: `self` refers to the object itself, so methods can read and change that object's attributes.

questions.question: What does `AttributeError: 'Dog' object has no attribute 'name'` mean?
questions.explanation: Attributes only exist once assigned, typically in `__init__`.

questions.question: When does `__init__` run?
options: Automatically when an object is created
When you call it manually only
questions.explanation: `Dog("Rex", 3)` creates the object and calls `__init__` for you.

questions.question: What is wrong with `def __init__(name): ...` inside a class?
options: It lacks `self` as the first parameter
questions.explanation: Every instance method, including `__init__`, needs `self` first.

questions.question: Which attribute is shared by ALL objects of a class?
options: a class attribute defined in the class body
questions.explanation: Class attributes belong to the class and are visible through every instance.

questions.question: Which decorator defines an alternative constructor that receives the class?
questions.explanation: `@classmethod` methods get `cls` and can build objects, like `Student.from_string(...)`.

questions.question: A `@staticmethod` receives...
questions.explanation: A static method is just a function grouped inside the class.

questions.question: Given `class A: def one(self): return 1` and `def two(self): return one() + 1`, why does `two` fail?
questions.explanation: Inside a class you must call sibling methods through `self`.

questions.question: What does a leading underscore in `_balance` communicate?
options: It is meant for internal use
questions.explanation: It is a naming convention: "please do not touch from outside".

questions.question: What happens to `self.__secret` inside class `Person`?
questions.explanation: Name mangling makes accidental access harder; it is not real security.

questions.question: What does `@property` allow?
options: Reading a method result like an attribute, with optional validation on assignment
questions.explanation: Properties give attribute-style access with getter/setter logic behind the scenes.

questions.question: What happens when you assign to a property that has no setter?
questions.explanation: A read-only property raises `AttributeError` on assignment.

questions.question: What is the main reason to encapsulate data?
options: Prevent invalid states by controlling access
questions.explanation: Going through methods lets the class enforce its own rules.

questions.question: Which line makes `Dog` inherit from `Animal`?
questions.explanation: The parent class goes in brackets after the child's name.

questions.question: What does `super().__init__(name)` do in a child class?
questions.explanation: It lets the parent set up its part of the object.

questions.question: For `rex = Dog()` where `Dog` inherits `Animal`, what is `isinstance(rex, Animal)`?
questions.explanation: An object of a child class is also an instance of its parents.

questions.question: What is method overriding?
options: Defining two methods with the same name in one class
A child class redefining a method inherited from its parent
questions.explanation: The child's version is used for child objects.

questions.question: What is polymorphism?
options: The same method call behaving differently depending on the object
questions.explanation: Calling `animal.speak()` on different animals gives different results.

questions.question: What is duck typing?
options: An object is usable if it has the needed methods, regardless of its class
questions.explanation: Python cares about behaviour (methods), not the declared type.

questions.question: Which makes a method that subclasses MUST override?
questions.explanation: An abstract base class cannot be instantiated until abstract methods are implemented.

questions.question: Which dunder method controls what `print(obj)` shows?
questions.explanation: `__str__` returns the user-friendly text; `__repr__` is the developer-oriented form.

questions.question: Which method makes `a + b` work for your class?
questions.explanation: `a + b` calls `a.__add__(b)`.

questions.question: Which special method lets `len(obj)` work?
questions.explanation: Define `__len__` to return the size.

questions.question: What should `__add__` normally return?
questions.explanation: Operators should not mutate their operands; return a new object.

questions.question: A `Car` needs an `Engine`. Which design is best?
options: Car has an `engine` attribute holding an Engine object
questions.explanation: "Has-a" relationships are modelled with composition.

questions.question: What does `@dataclass` generate for you?
questions.explanation: It removes repetitive boilerplate for data-holding classes.

questions.question: How should a dataclass declare a list default?
questions.explanation: Mutable defaults are rejected; `default_factory` gives every object its own list.
